speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In an effort to maintain the relevance and sustainability of our healthcare system, MOH earlier outlined its chief strategies to transform our healthcare system to meet the challenges of the future with three key shifts.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over the past few years, the focus on health promotion and maintenance has been unrelenting and I applaud all Singaporeans for rising to this challenge.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The call to arms to fight diabetes has reverberated through our society.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We are all exercising more, eating more brown rice, for instance, saying "no" to sugar and "no" to over-eating.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I appreciate the many initiatives and the nudges that we are making to make Singaporeans choose a healthier lifestyle.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For instance, where I work, all of the kopitiams and coffee-shops no longer put sugar in their beverages of coffee and tea.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If you want to, you actually have to add it yourself.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is initiatives and small little measures like these that will help our fight forward.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I look forward to more initiatives from MOH and the Health Promotion Board (HPB) to promote healthy living in Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As in every battle, it would be a mistake to step back when the tide is in our favour.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have voiced my strong support for the right citing of medical care to the community wherever possible and, for this to be possible, we have to continue strengthening both our primary care and intermediate and long-term care (ILTC) sectors.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I will speak on primary care transformation later.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But at this juncture, I would just like to ask: are our efforts to increase ILTC manpower and infrastructure on track, as detailed in the 2020 Masterplan?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This call to shift from hospital to community also heralds another key theme that was announced in this year's Budget Statement.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many Members have already spoken on this, but I was heartened, like the rest, by the announcements that health and social services will be more closely integrated.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is because there is clear evidence from around the world that the health of an individual is closely related to one's socioeconomic status.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A recent study from the United States (US), using data from the Centres for Disease Control, confirmed that people with higher incomes lived longer and had better health scores in virtually every parameter.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One commentator went so far as to suggest that "being rich is the best healthcare plan that America has to offer".

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There could be many reasons why people with lower incomes have poorer health scores.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The most obvious would be access to healthcare, but this is probably less true in Singapore than in other countries because our comprehensive healthcare system with universal coverage and very targeted subsidies has tended to flatten inequities in medical coverage.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Poorer health has also been associated with educational level which, itself, correlates with lower income.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: People with lower educational status, however, are not necessarily less knowledgeable about health, compared to those with higher education.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We all appreciate that one of the most important paths to good health is to exercise good food choices.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One study looked at why children coming from wealthier, better-educated parents grew up preferring healthier foods and were ultimately healthier.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important before we go in to understand that where children are concerned, research has shown that kids might actually need to try a new type of food, about eight or up to 15 times, before they can accept it and perhaps grow to like it.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, what the researchers found was that while parents from all backgrounds understood which foods were healthy and which were not, eat more vegetables, less fried foods and so on and sweets, parents who were less educated and with lower incomes often did not persist in offering healthier foods to their kids.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This could be because of the steep upfront cost in introducing these foods to children.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If a parent who is already working within a tight budget and time is short and a child refuses broccoli, for instance, then they will be less likely to persist with it because the child will probably refuse and it will end up on the floor.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They would soon give up and say, "Okay, maybe we will just give them the chicken nuggets that they are clamouring for".

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A family which is wealthier may perhaps have the luxury to be able to continue offering this food, even though the broccoli ends up on the floor 10 or 15 times, until the child learns to appreciate it.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In line with this, let me call on the Ministry to continue working with MOE and our schools to ensure that only healthy foods be served to our children.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand the constraints that some families will face in regard to food choices at home, but I hope that our schools can play a bigger role towards inculcating healthy eating habits in our young.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I feel that this should actually start at the preschool level, rather than just at the primary school level.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some years ago, a team from the Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health worked with myself and my grassroots volunteers to conduct a health survey in one area of Queenstown.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The researchers actually found that this difference was not due to any knowledge gaps.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If you ask people from all educational levels whether they knew what mammography was and why it was important, I think the knowledge was the same.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Whether you came from a low or high educational background, you understood the importance of it.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the meantime, I hope that this new compact between our social and health services will allow us to dive deep into the social circumstances of our lower-income fellow Singaporeans to give them the support that they need to achieve a long and healthy life.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that the Ministry would be able to share more about the proposed integration of health and social services, as I feel that this would go a long way towards flattening the social gradients in the health of our population.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is a tricky subject, because what is value in healthcare?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Just as the quality of health services is sometimes difficult to quantify, what represents good value in medical care?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Of course, value is important because, if we are counting our pennies, we have to ensure that healthcare remains affordable by ensuring that we get the best outcomes for the lowest financial outlay.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Value-driven healthcare policies could be a significant avenue of ensuring the sustainability of our system.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can I ask if this has led to any desired gains in efficiency and value of care delivery?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some interventions may seem very promising but with uncertain benefits, and they are controversial.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, for things like hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, at which point do we actually choose to treat otherwise healthy individuals with medications, new technologies, remote consultations?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some studies have shown that although it is easier, but it tended to increase the utilisation of services with no discernable improvements in health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   A good healthcare delivery system has to be supported by robust infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do we make sure that we have enough beds in our hospitals, nursing homes and care centres to meet the increasing demand of our ageing population?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Their grievances range from an unexpected death in hospital, to a physical accident while conveying a patient, causing patient injury.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In cases of unexpected death, the Coroner and the Police are likely to be activated, ensuring a strong measure of independence into the inquiry.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, in non-fatal cases, the hospital is usually the one which conducts an investigation or review into the incident.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As the hospitals are investigating their own handling of patients, a question that arises would be: what safeguards are there to ensure there is independence injected into the review process?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How far is input from patients or next-of-kin sought in such investigations?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will the patient or his representative have the opportunity to contradict evidence presented by the staff?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What role does the Ministry itself play in ensuring that hospital investigations are fair and transparent to patients?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In a 2004 article entitled "Quest for Quality Care and Patient Safety", MK Lim of the National University of Singapore (NUS) Faculty of Medicine noted that Singapore had more than 10 years ago, moved to a broader concept of quality assurance in healthcare that included the monitoring of clinical indicators and medical errors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to him, what was lacking then included public involvement and patient empowerment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Have we made any improvements in these areas?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that MOH has since moved on and now has a healthcare performance group that oversees clinical quality and care effectiveness.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Ministry tell us more about the priorities of this group?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, Sir, personalised medicine which involves the customisation of medical treatments to specific patient groups based on genetic profiles, seems to be a fast-emerging field of clinical research and application in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: But I believe the general public knows very little about this.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: There is, for example, the National Precision Medicine Initiative, which appears to need supercomputing resources to gather the genomic information of the whole Singapore and Southeast Asian populations to determine genetic risk and other personalised treatment.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister share more about the National Precision Medicine Initiative and whether MOH has oversight of the Initiative and its programmes?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: What is the long-term plan for the development of precision medicine in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Will a national registry of genetic disorders be developed?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: If so, how will it be used and how will the data be shared, nationally and internationally?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Does precision medicine research here involve deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) editing?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: If so, what are the bio-ethical rules governing the research?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It was reported in The Straits Times in August last year that hundreds of patients have already benefited from personalised medicine treatments in Tan Tock Seng Hospital, KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital (KKH) and Singapore General Hospital (SGH).

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The fee guidelines are expected to be published sometime this year.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The intention is to rein in escalating healthcare costs and ensure that medical services and goods remain affordable and accessible to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: What is the status of MOH's review on the HITF's report and recommendations?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Over the years, MOH has liberalised the use of MediSave for outpatient medical costs, and I would like to ask if MOH would consider further enhancements to the Chronic Disease Management Programme (CDMP) and also the Flexi-MediSave Scheme, which allows the elderly to utilise more of their MediSave for outpatient medical expenses.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Will the Ministry consider raising the Flexi-MediSave sum?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Would MOH consider liberalising the use of MediSave for the cost of other allied services, such as physiotherapy, or perhaps the use of consumables for chronic conditions like heart disease and diabetes?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: As I often call for during the COS debate, I would like to ask the Ministry to include more chronic conditions under CDMP.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I have always felt that this is an excellent programme and feel that it should be expanded wherever possible.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Including more conditions beyond the 19 already included will reduce the cash outlay required and encourage patients to be more compliant with treatment.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: I would also like to renew my call for the CDMP withdrawal limit to be calibrated to the number of chronic conditions that a patient has.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Thus, a patient suffering from three chronic illnesses should perhaps be allowed to withdraw a little bit more than a patient who only has one chronic illness.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   Raising special needs children comes with a lot of challenges.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Undoubtedly, it can be financially straining to families and parents who are taking care of these children.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even though Singapore has a support system that helps to lighten their load, there will still be occasions where it can be financially draining, especially when paying for the costs of medical treatment for these special needs children.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Recently, one of my residents with moderate income had to postpone the basic dental treatment for his special needs children due to the high cost since the children had to be administered with general anaesthesia.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These problems do surface when caring for special needs children.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Would MOH look into the possibility of allowing such parents to tap on their MediSave account to pay for the outpatient treatment for those who have special needs children, if the bill exceeds a certain amount?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Members from the Auto-immune Illness Support Group Singapore have bravely shared with me about their conditions, which are lifelong, chronic and not curable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They can only manage their symptoms by regular doctor visits and long-term medications, without which it can result in serious complications and prolonged hospitalisation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Because of individual reactions to medications, some have no choice but to take high-cost, non-subsidised medications.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Based on an internal survey by the group, there is a huge range and no single most common auto-immune condition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry consider including more auto-immune conditions into CDMP, allowing patients to use their MediSave and relieve their financial burden?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, some vaccines, like pneumococcal and human papillomavirus (HPV), are not subsidised but can be paid for using MediSave.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Minister Gan said, in reply to Mr Low Thia Khiang at last year's COS, that Government MediSave top-ups can be used to pay for vaccines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, many Singaporeans may not want to use MediSave for vaccines, preferring to keep the MediSave for bigger bills incurred later in life.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Based on these two actions and their results, my suggestion is that MOH can introduce targeted subsidies to greatly reduce the price of vaccines if there is evidence that this would stimulate higher take-up and not only reduce disease incidence later in life but reap long-term cost savings for the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But as it turns out, I do not have to implore for a third time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With the implementation of the new system, we would be removing an anomaly that has previously existed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Depending on circumstances, many mentally disabled persons are effectively in the same position as young children as they can only perform ADL under supervision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Yet, their caregivers did not get the levy concessions and grants that caregivers of young children did.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am sure these affected caregivers will warmly welcome this announcement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Assoc Prof Faishal announced that the evaluation of support level for mentally challenged care recipients will be done at Day Activity Centres and Therapy Hubs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It seems to me that appropriate resources and tools would have to be provided to the Day Activity Centres and Therapy Hubs so that they can better assess the mentally challenged care recipient's needs level.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The officers would have to contend with a wide spectrum of mental conditions, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would welcome MOH's elaboration on the system that will be implemented in three weeks' time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Without a doubt, though, we are moving in the right direction.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, can you take both cuts together?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, Sir, we have many agencies and programmes promoting mental well-being and assisting Singaporeans with mental health issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The National Council of Social Service (NCSS) publishes the Mental Health Resource Directory on its website.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Directory is 60 pages long and there are 11 helplines listed in it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With these programmes and resources, we have the elements of a mental health support system in place in Housing and Development Board (HDB) estates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By themselves, the programmes and resources can be too complex for a person with mental health issues to navigate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The next step, thus, is to bring the elements together and integrate them to build a system that is easily accessible to people with mental health issues or their family, with a No Wrong Door policy to direct persons to the most appropriate help.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just as AIC has been designated as the central agency to coordinate diverse senior care services to better deliver care to our seniors, should there be a central agency to coordinate mental health care services?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the network of Social Service Offices (SSOs) under MSF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would it make sense for MOH to partner MSF to leverage the SSOs to coordinate mental health care services in the heartlands?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Dementia is the most prevalent neuro-degenerative disease that affects an estimated one in 10 people aged over 60.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There were over 40,000 seniors suffering from dementia in 2016.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is expected to rise to 92,000 by 2030.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Dementia poses significant health and socio-economic burdens to patients and caregivers and to society as a whole.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Countries like Korea, Japan and Australia are implementing similar high-level plans, making dementia a public health priority.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These plans include accessible early detection services, access to information, pre- and post-diagnosis care and support, as well as supporting people with dementia in aged communities to remain socially engaged and active.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2016, AIC was discussing plans with stakeholders to develop a national registry of dementia patients so that they can be more easily located if they go missing and their caregivers contacted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, these plans were put on hold last year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Minister give an account of why the plans were put on hold?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Were there issues with getting the consent of families?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Were there issues with implementation linked to the registry held by the Neighbourhood Police Centre in Yishun, as part of the dementia-friendly community initiative launched there in 2016?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the plans for a national registry be revived?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There are a few types of dementia and it is possible to lower the risk of dementia through lifestyle choices and habits, such as staying mentally active, socially engaged and physically active.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Knowing the warning signs and symptoms of dementia can help patients and their families discover their condition earlier and help them better manage.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: MOH has previously launched a few dementia friendly communities (DFCs) where the community at large knows what dementia is and better support the persons and their caregivers.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Can MOH give us an update on DFC's efforts and what plans does the Ministry have in the pipeline to further enhance our current efforts to better cope with the higher number of Singaporeans with dementia?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They may suffer from depression, memory loss and dementia.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This poses a challenge not only to the seniors but also to their caregivers and family members.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their mental illness can result in their being isolated from the society.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We are already seeing cases of our elderly living alone, perhaps because the spouses have passed on, and gradually they go into depression and some would be gripped by dementia.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some have no relatives or friends to care for them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They become dependent on social workers and the community volunteers to give them the support in their twilight years.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to prepare ourselves for more of such cases, as improved medical care is seeing people living longer lives.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: As this is a labour-intensive sector, our manpower shortage has to be overcome through enhancing productivity and innovation.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: How is MOH encouraging innovation and spurring productivity in the healthcare sector?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Would the Minister elaborate on process improvements which have contributed to better patient care and experience and boost productivity gains in different segments of our medical sector?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Tremendous gains are being made every day in the fields of robotics, artificial intelligence (AI), big data analytics and the Internet of Things (IoT).

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: These have the potential to vastly improve healthcare delivery and outcomes.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: How are we leveraging such positive disruptions in healthcare services for Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Would the Minister share an update on the investments the Government is making to boost automation and tap upon new and innovative technologies to provide quality, affordable healthcare?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Increasingly, the healthcare sector will have to work closely with diverse fields, such as information technology (IT), engineering and biotech, to come up with innovative healthcare solutions but, at the same time, without losing the human touch.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: What are some of our local success stories in innovative research and cross-sector collaboration?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I declare that I am the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of an international research consultancy whose Korean arm has researched this subject.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In Korea, private sector Silver Towns emerged in the 1990s.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Initially, they were driven by big conglomerates or chaebols, which developed a site for senior residences but also built in proximate facilities like retail, personal services, sports and recreation facilities and even, in some cases, childcare and play facilities for the grandchildren when children visit their parents.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Korean Silver Town model emphasises high-rise, high-density living, integrating smart technology, which is a little different from the assisted living and retirement community models seen elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There are different Silver Towns in Korea with different mixes of facilities catering to different price points.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Silver Towns embody a balanced point between, on the one hand, personal independence and freedom to seniors and, on the other hand, the presence of medical staff, facilities and the most structured daily routine administered by professionals for those seniors who need it, such as those having dementia.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I do not suggest Silver Towns as a substitute to seniors staying with their children.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: However, for some seniors, this is not possible while, for others, this is not desirable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, Silver Towns could be part of the ecosystem, catering to the needs of our seniors, offering one option for living arrangements.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Lest I be misunderstood, I do not advocate that Silver Towns be run by the Government, as some are in Korea, or come with 100% subsidies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The roadmap to this could be, after the concept has been studied, to issue a tender to invite master developers to build and operate a Silver Town.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: A pilot project could be used to test demand.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Means-tested subsidies could perhaps be applied in some cases.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Government could also nudge Silver Towns to become testbeds for the trial of new, disruptive concepts catering to the senior community and make it convenient for non-government organisations (NGOs) to target and trial programmes aimed at seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: Recently, private companies have been taking over the operations of nursing homes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: My main concern is whether the objectives and goals of the private companies are able to be aligned with the business model of the nursing home.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: If the profit maximisation approach is adopted by these companies, then we could see the undesirable rise in charges that will inevitably drive up the cost of nursing care.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui
text: When needed, how does MOH get the private nursing homes to meet changing trends to include new services that the nursing homes might not previously have, services, such as home personal care, home nursing or nursing posts to help residents change bandages and so on?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But much of these actions are augmenting the support rather than preventive.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As we extensively focus on how to enable the Baby Boomers to age in place, we must begin thinking of strategies to ensure that the Generation X/Y is managing their health on a different trajectory, a trajectory where the starting point of their mental and health state are healthier, with lower dependence on medication and the need for longer-term care needs in future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It is common knowledge that we must eat well and exercise frequently to stay fit.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But apart from health campaigns or one-off activities like the National Step Challenge, Let Us Beat Diabetes, how has MOH engaged the Generation X/Y on a continuous basis to ensure that we have a future ageing population that is healthy?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Given the busy schedule of our young working adults, accessibility to exercises is critical.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The community exercise initiatives by HPB and Active SG are encouraging.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: It not only provides exercise options close to their homes but also encourages community bonding.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Is there any plan for MOH to keep this interest towards a healthy lifestyle more sustainable?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Variety and ready availability of food choices today have spoilt our consumers at a young age.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With their busy lifestyles, more families are dining out and consuming more, as shown in the National Nutrition Survey.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: While food preference may be individual, some policy adjustments can help with mindset change in dietary habits.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some areas for consideration I would like to put up are: (a) types of ready-processed food allowed to be sold in vending machines near the residential neighbourhood, medical facilities and Institutions of Higher Learning (IHLs); (b) proportion of meal sizes sold in hawker centres and food courts at commensurate prices; and (c) inculcating the concept of discipline in healthy food intake rather than mere caloric value of every bite.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As we understand there is a growing need for caregiving support to our elderly, we are constantly looking at ways to supplement this network of caregivers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This effort can enhance the supply and we must continue doing so.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But as we extend this support through FDWs to future robots, we should not forget the human touch.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Some of them had roles of caregiving to their families, and certainly many still bear the brunt of caring for their own children.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Their unfortunate family circumstances aside, these women require the necessary skills to gain confidence and rebuild their lives.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As a start, these beneficiaries can be assigned to work within the community where they live in.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The benefits are two-fold, as they can manage caring for their family and also be gainfully employed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Over time, I hope these women will also have more options in employment and can better care for their own elderly at home and be financially independent.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But there are those seniors whose annual value of property do not fall under the current criteria and may also face challenges.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: With the advent of technology, we should look beyond direct subsidies into social outcome to benefit the larger group of seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For example, social partnerships with the private sector in creating environment and alert tools from remote operating centres that can deploy assistance to those seniors in need.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Or to provide home-based care products and services, where it also monitors health and movement conditions of seniors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Another way is to create new funds for app developers who can create socially engaging apps aimed at active agers or to draw experience from those who understand the mindset of how an elderly reacts, for example, like Mdm Masako Wakamiya, 82 years old, who is one of the world's oldest app developers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: We should creatively generate options and create accommodative relief for individuals and families, rather than one where individuals are more likely to become supplicant recipients of charity.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, can you take both cuts together?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With an ageing population, there may soon be a point in time when there are more who need care than those who can care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Other concerns also include seeing more with age-related disabilities and loneliness, as more elderly outlive their family members or as more choose to remain single.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While the human touch in eldercare can never be fully substituted, we can leverage technology to mitigate some of these concerns.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: By leveraging technology and AI more effectively, we can drastically change how care is provided and help even more Singaporeans age in place.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At present, many of the technology-related pilots conducted are focused on making the living environment more enabling, which is the right thing to do.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am also aware that there are some solutions, such as telemedicine and marketplace applications, to help seniors live more conveniently.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But I hope we will also start exploring solutions that can provide effective and transformative interventions to help individual seniors live independently.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Japan is even further ahead of us in terms of ageing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They have an increasing number of elderly with a decreasing number of working adults.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They suffer severe labour shortage, especially in eldercare nursing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Yet, they reinvented how the elderly can be cared for by leveraging technology and AI.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From Toyota's Robina and Humanoid, Honda's ASIMO, Tokai's RIBA to AIST's PARO, which is a very cute seal, Japan has a full range of robots that can help the elderly with household chores, to get out of bed, conduct conversations complete with emotions and even help paraplegics walk again.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Imagine if these solutions are available to us in Singapore, many elderly whom we used to think can only be cared for in nursing homes, can now lead a fairly independent life in their own flats.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Alas, while these are possible and already in existence, it is still not known if these solutions can be exported and at what price.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Could we accelerate developments locally and implement sooner than later?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the drive towards a Smart Nation, how is the Ministry part of this effort and what other programmes or public-private partnerships might be available that can be utilised to further our agenda for seniors?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am also aware that the Government has been looking into ways to make our living environment more elderly-friendly with initiatives, such as City for All Ages, Enhancement for Active Seniors (EASE) and other general upgrading programmes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are great efforts in retrofitting hard environments to become more enabling.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, it is the details that often make the difference.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, designing with the elderly in mind, ensuring that products, services and the real or virtual environment that we are immersed in are inclusive and empowering is important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should design to include and empower our seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must not design only with the "majority" in mind, who used to be younger, and expect the rest to comply or find their own solution.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moreover, what is designed for the elderly, surely must be suitable for the young, too.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we should conscientiously and actively apply elderly-friendly designs into all our hardware and heartware solutions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One is the "Guidelines for age-friendly homes" and the other is the "Guidance for digital devices and online services to be senior friendly".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are a good start, but we need to mainstream elderly-friendly designs much more and make them pervasive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need to apply elderly-friendly designs to the development of common spaces, facilities, machine and application interfaces, workflows, public processes and more.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The key is to make them pervasive such that seniors can move from setting to setting smoothly and live a completely normal life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: No institution or country so far has been an authority in terms of setting elderly-friendly design standards.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore can take the lead in setting elderly-friendly standards and be the authority in this area.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Is there effort to train more students in elderly-friendly designs?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And perhaps, would the Government consider creating specialisations for students to undertake in tertiary institutions?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This will enable the long-term needs of our seniors to be catered more comprehensively.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: As I have said in my Budget speech, I hope MOH will spell its objectives clearly for a good outcome.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The operation details will need a lot of consideration and supervision.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: It will need the considered effort of Senior Activity Centres (SACs), stakeholders and staff to come on board with a shared mission.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Some centres may have become entrenched in their own ways of operation and MOH may face and need to address some resistance to change.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Thus, daily meals and activity programmes must be provided with an aim in mind, that is, to assist these seniors remain in the community and ward off frailty, diseases and immobility.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Are there enough personnel to take over the transfer from this April?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Is MOH poised to train present and future personnel to provide for these aged care services?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Community Aged Care Services will require many social and medical personnel, especially for seniors who are house-bound with partial or full disability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I hope MOH will spare no effort to provide these personnel as it will determine the outcome of these services.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Could MOH train healthcare workers and consider using not only full-time paid personnel but also family members, community volunteers and so on?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Healthcare aides can be trained for specific skills, like simple dressing of wounds, simple grooming, toe-nail cutting for non-diabetics using sterile techniques, assisting with feeding, catheter care, prosthesis use and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This will free up medical staff like the nurses.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I am also happy that AIC will act as the single agency on delivery of holistic aged care services to seniors across both the health and social domains.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Many seniors living alone with medical conditions and mobility problems can be managed at home with these holistic services.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Like the one at Chin Swee, AIC assists with the nurses and healthcare aide team that look into the needs of the seniors daily in supervising their medical conditions and daily living essentials.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This has enabled residents to have lesser frequency of hospital visits and enabled them to stay in their own homes despite their illnesses and immobility.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: With AIC under MOH being the agency in charge of SACs, I feel that we can achieve better preventive healthcare, meaning early detection and treatment with better follow-up of patients to achieve good outcomes in preventing irreversible medical conditions that result in permanent impairment in health and mobility.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I hope that such models of care can be expanded quickly as we are fighting a tide of the increasing numbers of seniors who can benefit from such holistic care services.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: There are health and social benefits in volunteering.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: It offers seniors significant physical, emotional and cognitive health benefits.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Could MOH provide a broader spectrum on the types of volunteering to attract more seniors?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Can these seniors be reimbursed for volunteerism similar to the Pioneer Generation (PG) ambassadors?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: I hope MOH will spare no effort in ensuring this new initiative takes off well, to enable seniors to stay healthier and happier and age more gracefully in place, living with their loved ones in their own homes, and in their familiar environment in the community.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, I hope the services provided are more holistic and sustainable.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Skills training with services for employment and employability and active ageing programmes can form part of this enhancement.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The one-stop service centres should be easily accessible near to the homes of the seniors, and the programmes should be cost-effective and affordable.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is important to care for the mental health of seniors.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: At age 65, some seniors may have retired or are about to retire.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Besides the loss of income, these seniors may also feel less purposeful and bored without daily work to occupy their time.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Willing seniors with capability to contribute can be assisted to transit into less demanding jobs with shorter working hours.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With their new-found time on hand, some seniors may also be interested to pick up new skills or knowledge.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This interest in lifelong learning should be encouraged and supplemented with learning institutions’ recommendation of courses based on individual interests.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This centre can also be a conduit to all relevant services that may be required by the seniors.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Some examples include providing awareness of advance care planning, lasting power of attorney (LPA) and understanding of the various Government schemes, such as ElderShield, MediShield and the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS).

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The current PG Ambassadors can help to support this one-stop service centre for seniors.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The seniors who benefited from the service centre are also the best ambassadors to encourage and guide other seniors to access the services provided.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: A volunteer network can also be developed among these seniors for them to give back in other areas of the community, such as healthcare.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is essential for a well-established facility to be complemented by professionals.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As such, it is equally important to ensure that the support staff running these service centres are adequately equipped to support seniors, attend compulsory training in basic geriatric services, have relevant language proficiency and are able to identify mental health issues among seniors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Chairman, first, let me thank all the Members for their comments and the suggestions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our population is ageing rapidly, with a growing chronic disease burden.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We want to not just live long but also live well.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To do that, each of us must also do our best to adopt a healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We also need a good healthcare system that is both accessible and affordable.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked about our progress on Healthcare 2020 which outlined our strategy to improve accessibility, quality and affordability of healthcare.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have made good progress but much needs to be done from now until 2020 and beyond.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Over the next few years, we will continue to add healthcare facilities across Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To the north, we are developing Woodlands Health Campus, which will be ready progressively from 2022.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Down south, we are developing Outram Community Hospital and the new National Cancer Centre as part of the redevelopment of the Outram Campus.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In the north-east, we are on track to open Sengkang Hospitals later this year.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The new Changi General Hospital Medical Centre in the east will also be ready this year.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In the west, we look forward to the new Centre for Oral Health at the National University Hospital (NUH).

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Not forgetting the central region, where the Integrated Care Hub and National Centre for Infectious Diseases are being built at Novena.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To support ageing in the community, we have also added 4,200 home-based and 2,900 centre-based care places.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have also grown our healthcare workforce by about 25,000, or about 36%, since 2011.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To ensure healthcare remains affordable to Singaporeans, we increased subsidies at outpatient clinics and enhanced CHAS for primary care, commonly known as the Blue Card and the Orange Card.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In 2015, we introduced MediShield Life for inpatient care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are also investing in a future-ready workforce that will anchor the transformation of our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor will elaborate on our plans to grow and upskill our healthcare manpower later.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We need to innovate and find new ways to deliver quality care to patients in a more effective and efficient way and for better outcomes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, at Pioneer Polyclinic, which opened in July 2017, patients are cared for by a team comprising doctors, nurses and allied health professionals.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Having a regular primary care team will ensure better continuity of care for patients.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is one of the many initiatives that has improved the quality of care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At 4.6% of gross domestic product (GDP), this is lower than most developed countries, but we expect this to rise over time as our population ages.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: On the other hand, Government expenditure on health grew twice as fast, by about 120% over the same period, to fund infrastructure investments and to keep healthcare affordable for Singaporeans, by reducing their share of out-of-pocket expenses from about 40% to 30%.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: With the introduction of the PG Package and MediShield Life and the extended use of MediSave, the out-of-pocket for eight in 10 subsidised hospitalisation bills was below $100.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But we cannot simply keep increasing subsidy or insurance payouts.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Higher insurance payouts will result in higher premiums or higher subsidies will need to be funded.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: All these will be borne by Singaporeans eventually through higher premiums and higher taxes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, we need to take a long-term view on this.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Even as we implement Healthcare 2020, we need to look beyond 2020 and make three key shifts to ensure our healthcare system is future-ready.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Three Beyonds, which Dr Chia Shi-Lu reminded us about, provided the roadmap to a sustainable system beyond Healthcare 2020.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First, we are going Beyond Hospital to the Community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Over the last decade, we have increased our total spending in the primary care and ILTC sectors by close to four times, from $1.3 billion in FY2007-2011 to $5.1 billion in FY2012-2016.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These investments reflect our priority to anchor care firmly in the community.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As we continue to invest in community care, we also need to bring social and healthcare services closer to better serve our people.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This has led to the formation of the Silver Generation Office (SGO) as well as expansion of Community Networks for Seniors (CNS), which I elaborated earlier in my speech on SG Cares.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Senior Minister of State Lam Pin Min will share later how we are strengthening primary care for the future.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Six new polyclinics are being built under Healthcare 2020; two are already open, and four more to come by 2020.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will add another six to eight new polyclinics by 2030.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is part of our commitment to ensure Singaporeans can access primary care closer to their homes.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are not just building polyclinics; we are also partnering private GPs through the Primary Care Networks (PCN) to offer subsidised team-based care in the community under CHAS.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Our second shift, Beyond Quality to Value, plays a pivotal role in ensuring sustainability.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We established ACE to provide guidance on cost-effective drugs and treatment, and I thank Dr Chia Shi-Lu for supporting the work of ACE.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We also introduced the Healthcare Productivity Fund to spur productivity improvement efforts in our healthcare institutions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Mr Chairman, co-payment has been an integral feature throughout all our healthcare schemes, including MediShield Life as well as IPs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It plays an important role in ensuring our healthcare system is sustainable by emphasising personal responsibility in healthcare, by encouraging service providers to focus on appropriate and cost-effective interventions, and by nudging patients to make prudent decisions in healthcare services.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is important as it ensures that all stakeholders, including patients, have a stake in their decision.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As Dr Chia Shi-Lu pointed out, some private insurance policies offer zero co-payment coverage.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Such riders encourage a "buffet syndrome" as patients do not need to pay anything when they receive medical treatment.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It undermines the co-payment principle and dilutes the personal responsibility to choose appropriate and necessary care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat will elaborate more.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This will encourage responsible behaviour by both patients and healthcare providers.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will continue to review our healthcare financing policies to ensure that co-payment remains affordable, through targeted subsidies, MediSave use and for those who still have difficulties, MediFund will be a safety net.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: No one will be denied appropriate healthcare because they cannot afford to pay.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: But ultimately, the best way to beat rising healthcare costs is to stay healthy.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is a focus of our final shift Beyond Healthcare to Health.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin will give an update on WoD and detail how we are encouraging and supporting healthier lifestyles.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will create a supportive environment for Singaporeans to lead healthy lives, but each of us must do our part.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These three shifts will be a multi-year effort.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To support these initiatives, we have taken the first steps to reorganise ourselves.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The bad news is that this is not the end.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In fact, this is just the beginning of a long journey to create synergy and deliver better care for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: A patient, Mr H, 73 years old, was admitted to SGH after a fall last year.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Besides rehabilitation treatment for his fall, he also needed to manage his diabetes and hypertension.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Miss Siti Hajar, a Patient Navigator and experienced nurse from SGH, coordinated both his health and social care even after he has been discharged.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Miss Siti visited him fortnightly and ensured that his chronic conditions are well-managed from home.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As Mr H lives alone in his flat in Kaki Bukit, the CGH Community Care team – now part of the SingHealth team – was activated to accompany him for follow-ups at Bedok Polyclinic and arranged for home help services for him.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I am pleased to know that Mr H's condition has now stabilised, and the SingHealth team continues to provide him with strong support.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is what reclustering is all about – bringing healthcare institutions and the community closer together to provide good, seamless care for patients, such as Mr H, and many others.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Another example of this synergy is the new national integrated supply chain we are setting up.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This goes beyond the Group Procurement Office currently run by SingHealth.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It pools the whole supply chain's functions, including procurement and resources of the three clusters, together to achieve economies of scale, create greater synergy, develop new capabilities and evolve innovative supply chain solutions.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This will yield system-level gains for patients, providers and staff.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This will also help to mitigate cost increases and bring greater convenience to patients.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Advances in medical science, increasing digitalisation and connectivity hold tremendous promises for rethinking healthcare.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: MOHT will focus on longer-term ideas that can be scaled up for system-level transformation.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some of these ideas will be tested at the health empowering Alexandra Hospital campus which the National University Health System (NUHS) will take over from the second half of 2018.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Similarly, we will be initiating the master planning of NUH's Kent Ridge Campus in the West, to see how Kent Ridge can be best positioned to meet future healthcare needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have already started some development at the Kent Ridge campus.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the end of the day, we must remember that the state of our health primarily depends on our choices.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As far as we can, we must choose to live healthily.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is the key not just to a sustainable healthcare system, but a vibrant society and good quality of life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: He is pursuing a sports diploma at Republic Polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Keeping fit is as much part of his work as it is his passion.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Not only is he enjoying the benefits of better health, but he is also going the extra mile to influence others.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: He persuaded his family to start eating brown rice, more fruits and more vegetables and less fried food.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: He exemplifies how taking ownership of one's health can have a ripple effect, to better the lives of many more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, a key priority for MOH is to keep our healthcare system sustainable and affordable for this generation and future generations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I will elaborate on our efforts to achieve this outcome under the three Ps: Productivity, Partnerships and Prevention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked how MOH encourages healthcare innovation and productivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We set up the Healthcare Tripartite Committee for Workforce Innovation and Productivity in 2016.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Committee has reviewed rules and policies based on ground feedback to streamline work processes, encourage adoption of smart technology and empower different groups of healthcare workers to maximise their contributions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOH introduced the Healthcare Productivity Fund (HPF) in 2012.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: More than 250 projects have been implemented so far, benefiting over 70 public healthcare and community care organisations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Use of smart technologies will be integrated in existing and upcoming public healthcare facilities to increase system-level productivity, improve patient care and prepare our healthcare facilities for the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The productivity efforts extend beyond hospitals to the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: AIC will collaborate with providers to redesign traditionally manpower-intensive processes, such as rehabilitation and showering.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: AIC will also help providers to adopt assistive equipment, such as ceiling hoists, to ease the physical strain on our healthcare workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I will now speak on the next P: Partnerships.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Besides working closely with public healthcare institutions, we collaborate with private sector providers to tap on their expertise and resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the ILTC sector, MOH invites VWOs and private operators to tender for operating rights at our Build-Own-Lease (BOL) facilities, and we partner private operators to provide subsidised nursing home care through the Portable Subsidy Scheme (PSS).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: BOL and PSS operators are appointed via competitive requests-for-proposal, where operators propose and commit to their fees and charges for subsidised residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Miss Cheng Li Hui said, this can help to ensure prices for quality care remain reasonable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOH supports providers, including private nursing homes, with manpower development and productivity initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, partnerships also mean all stakeholders – patients and caregivers, healthcare providers and professionals, insurers and employers, and the Government – working together on a common goal to keep healthcare costs sustainable and affordable for everyone over the longer term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At the most fundamental level, it is in the philosophy and design of our healthcare financing system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: During the Budget Debate, Ms Sylvia Lim asked if the higher MediShield Life deductible for older policyholders was a form of "reverse discrimination".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We should look at the complete picture rather than focus on a single observation in isolation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The MediShield Life Review Committee wanted MediShield Life to be a basic health insurance plan for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The objective was to provide coverage for large hospital bills based on inpatient treatment at subsidised wards, as well as costly outpatient treatments like dialysis and chemotherapy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For the scheme to remain sustainable, premiums are computed to be actuarially sound.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government then provides means-tested subsidies and additional premium support to ensure that premiums remain affordable for lower- and middle-income Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On MediShield Life deductibles, the amount is set for each policy year and not for each treatment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The deductible amount can be paid using MediSave and Singaporeans who require further financial support can approach our medical social workers for assistance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As older policyholders incur higher medical bills in each policy year compared to younger cohorts, their premiums are higher to reflect the larger and more frequent claims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There is a trade-off between the deductible amount and premiums, with lower deductible amounts resulting in higher premiums.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Recognising that policyholders will pay higher premiums as they age, the Government has provided higher MediShield Life premium subsidies for older Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is in line with the progressive design of our healthcare financing system, with more Government subsidies going to older Singaporeans and those from lower- and middle-income families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Besides higher MediShield Life premium subsidies, they also receive 50% more subsidies in polyclinics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For PG, they enjoy further benefits, such as special CHAS subsidies at GP clinics, additional MediShield Life premium subsidies and MediSave top-ups every year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, rather than having "reverse discrimination" against older Singaporeans, our healthcare system is, in fact, providing them with more financial subsidies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We do the same for the lower- and middle-income Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singaporeans support this financing approach because it is consistent with our values to build a fair and just society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, beyond healthcare financing, partnership amongst all stakeholders is also needed to ensure that quality care is delivered at sustainable and affordable cost for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Last year, the Singapore Medical Council revised their ethical guidelines for doctors indicating that fees paid to Third-Party Administrators must not be based on a proportion of the doctor's fees, or what is commonly known as "fee splitting".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is to prevent unnecessary inflation of healthcare costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The purpose is to encourage appropriate charging by healthcare providers and enable patients and payers to make better informed decisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As I have said in this House at a previous Sitting, most of our doctors do charge appropriately, as they have their patients' well-being at heart.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But for the ones who charge excessive fees, please know that MOH is monitoring and will take action against doctors who overcharge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: During the Budget Debate, Ms Sylvia Lim suggested reviewing medical insurance schemes to include deductibles and co-payments, to discourage over-consumption and inefficient use of resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This was similar to the earlier recommendations from HITF which Dr Chia Shi-Lu has asked for an update.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Every Singaporean Citizen and Permanent Resident (PR) is covered by MediShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Today, about two in three Singapore residents have also bought IPs, and these are private insurance products that offer added coverage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Both MediShield Life and IPs have co-payment features in the form of deductibles and co-insurance, and their premiums can be paid using MediSave.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Among those who have bought IPs, some have paid additional cash, for what is known as "full riders".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These cover the entire co-payment under the IP plan so that the policyholder ends up paying nothing, regardless of the bill size.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As highlighted in the HITF's report, the zero co-payment feature of these full riders has resulted in the buffet syndrome, leading to over-consumption, over-servicing and over-charging of healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Some of the examples of over-consumption and over-servicing are, to put it plainly, disturbing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In one case, a full rider policyholder made claims for 12 nose scopes in a year without clear medical need.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We also have patients who are admitted for gastritis or piles and then referred to many other specialties ranging from dermatology, ophthalmology, ear, nose and throat, and orthopaedics, for additional scans and tests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Up to $25,000 for a hospital stay that was less than 24 hours.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There was also a full rider policyholder who underwent an expensive surgery for a small breast lump removal that cost $70,000 in doctor's fees alone, when there was an equally effective alternative procedure which costs only $5,000.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To be fair, not all doctors prescribed such expensive treatments, and not all full rider policyholders submit such large claims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But it is clear that full riders have a detrimental impact on overall healthcare cost in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is a key reason why rider premiums have increased by up to 225% over the past two years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The negative impact of the zero co-payment feature extends beyond full rider policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over the last two years, IP premiums have also risen by up to 80%, with older policyholders and those on private hospital plans experiencing higher increases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If this trend continues, I am worried that IP and rider policyholders will find their insurance premiums increasingly unaffordable as they age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The zero co-payment feature of riders also pushes up healthcare costs in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over-consumption, over-servicing, over-charging of healthcare services will lead to faster and larger increases in overall healthcare expenditure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These increases will ultimately be borne by all Singaporeans through higher medical fees, insurance premiums and taxes, which all of us will pay directly or indirectly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, I am glad there is support from both sides of the House on the need for co-payment to keep healthcare expenditures sustainable and affordable for all Singaporeans over the longer term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Salma Khalik has also written an insightful piece in today's Straits Times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have to make a change now to prevent the problem from becoming worse in future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In line with the HITF’s recommendation, MOH will issue the following requirements for all new rider plans with immediate effect.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To address concerns from some policyholders that they may face high co-payment amounts due to the unlikely event of very large bills, the new riders will have a cap on the co-payment amount each year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Most insurers are planning to launch their new riders with an annual cap of $3,000, though they are allowed to set higher thresholds.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This places an upper limit on the risk exposure of policyholders, to protect them against very large bills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: New riders will be available within a year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Once the new riders are ready, these policyholders can choose to switch to the new riders earlier if they wish to do so, and any pre-existing conditions that are covered prior the switch will not be excluded.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We expect the new riders to have lower premiums than full riders, so the switch will result in premium savings for policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our objective is to address the concerns with overconsumption, over-servicing and overcharging as these will lead to patients and policyholders paying rapidly escalating fees and premiums over time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will be an unsustainable and undesirable outcome for Singapore, especially when we are ageing as a society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Policyholders can continue to tap on MediSave to pay for their co-payment amounts under the new riders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Three quarters of inpatient bills would have co-payment of $250 or less.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Nine in 10 inpatient bills would have a co-payment of $550 or less.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The 5% co-payment can be covered within the current MediSave withdrawal limits for 99% of all inpatient bills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For private hospital inpatient bills, in 2016, one in two would have a co-payment of $380 or less.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Three in four would have a co-payment of $670 or less, and nine in 10 would have a co-payment of $1,270 or less.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The above requirements will apply to new rider policies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We recognise that existing rider policies are commercial contracts between insurers and their policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If insurers intend to make changes to their existing policies, they should consider the interest and well-being of all policyholders as they seek to keep premiums affordable for everyone in the longer term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The requirements for new riders will not affect MediShield Life and IPs which already have co-payment features.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For patients who face financial difficulties with their bills, MediFund remains available as a safety net to ensure they continue to have access to quality subsidised healthcare in our public hospitals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: An important aspect of Prevention focuses on early screening and intervention.
