speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Last year, I announced the enhancements to the Screen for Life programme where eligible Singaporeans can have access to subsidised health screenings at a cost of $5, which includes the first post-screening consultation with a doctor.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: CHAS cardholders ‒ both orange and blue ‒ will pay $2, while the package is free for Pioneers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu asked whether the Ministry is considering further enhancements to CDMP as well as the Flexi-MediSave Scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I recalled Ms Thanaletchimi had raised a similar query during a previous COS debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: From June this year, MOH will make the following enhancements to CDMP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These will also broaden the coverage of our CHAS chronic subsidies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Based on current trends, one in three people with pre-diabetes could develop Type-2 diabetes within eight years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through early detection and intervention, we hope more patients with pre-diabetes can improve their condition and avoid developing diabetes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will benefit all our patients with IHD, even if their condition is not linked to diabetes or hypertension.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Third, we will enhance the support for diabetics who require insulin injections, as they require lancets and test strips to regularly monitor their blood glucose levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To support these patients, MOH will extend CDMP to lancets and test strips.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will take effect from June this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will also lower the eligible age for Flexi-MediSave, which is currently set at 65.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: From June this year, Singaporeans aged 60 and above can use up to $200 of their MediSave per year, for outpatient medical treatments at public sector Specialist Outpatient Clinics (SOCs), polyclinics and CHAS GPs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This expansion of Flexi-MediSave will benefit an additional 260,000 Singaporeans between the ages of 60 and 64.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To conclude, Mr Chairman, we need to transform our healthcare system so that it remains sustainable and affordable for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Everyone needs to play our part to stay healthy and prevent healthcare costs from rising too rapidly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Together, we can achieve better health and a better life for our people.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms K Thanaletchimi, can you take your second cut now.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: As such, will there be current jobs at risks and new jobs created across the healthcare sector?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: I applaud MOH for the efforts and training programmes it has introduced to attract Singaporeans into this sector in recent years, though more can be done.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: To further drive the success brought about by the existing MOH and AIC initiatives to bring locals into ILTC, I would like to suggest a holistic review of jobs, skills training, career progression and remuneration across this sector.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Jobs can be redesigned to create higher value jobs that provide areas of growth for the individuals.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: For example, in the public healthcare sector, HSEU had worked closely with the healthcare institutions to redesign the career pathway for Patient Service Associates (PSAs).

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: The process included multiple consultation sessions with our members to tailor the job role as they were the key stakeholders.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: It is essential for them to take ownership of their own future.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: The union helped to convince our members with the advantages of taking on larger specialised job roles to meet the changing needs of this sector so as to energise them with possible career progression and enhanced remuneration.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: With strong union-management collaboration, the redesigned career pathway for PSAs greatly enhanced the attractiveness of the job.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Concurrently, it has mitigated the possible redundancy for this group of employees whose jobs are increasingly at risk with the advent of technology.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: We should also look at other initiatives to attract back-to-work women, to encourage non-practising nurses to return to nursing and workers from other sectors to join through the Professional Conversion Programme (PCP).

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: Retiring healthcare workers in the mainstream of public healthcare institutions should also be given the option.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi
text: On this, I urge those who are in their early 50s and 40s to be engaged in the conversation as early as possible for second career options in ILTC.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: They are on the frontline every day, tending to the sick, counselling patients on their health, improving processes throughout the healthcare system, and the list goes on.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: With the push towards delivering greater quality and value in healthcare, the role of nurses is undoubtedly even more important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: We must, therefore, equip our nurses with adequate skills and knowledge to meet the increasing demands on them and also empower them to tackle the many difficult situations that they are faced with on a day-to-day basis.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Therefore, I would like to ask the Ministry for an update on the development and career pathways for our nurses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: As our public healthcare transforms, how will the role of nurses change and how will their training and career development transform along with it as well?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Chairman, one of the challenges facing the Ministry is that of getting sufficient healthcare workers, both frontline and backroom.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: This is especially so with the adding on of more healthcare facilities and the rising demands on our medical services.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: With tight manpower against high demand, it will mean longer queues and much inconvenience for the patients.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: The Ministry has succeeded in getting some retired nurses to come back.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Can I ask if the Minister would draw on the pool of retirees in Singapore and offer them a career path in the healthcare sector so that it is a mutually beneficial exercise?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: (In Mandarin):   Apart from welcoming retired nurses to come back to work, we can also encourage retirees or mid-career switchers to join the nursing industry.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Some women quit their job in order to look after the children or the elderly in the family.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: After their children have grown up, they may want to come back to the workforce.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: We should encourage these women to join the nursing industry.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: If these mid-career switchers and retirees can undergo relevant nursing training, they will be able to help to alleviate the manpower shortage issue in the healthcare sector.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Facilitating career advancement and training of allied healthcare workers will benefit many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, would the Minister for Health consider a central body which studies and charts career opportunities of the allied healthcare workers in each of the integrated healthcare clusters?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In a few short years, we have ramped up considerable infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, effective healthcare, especially to meet our ageing population, requires a well-trained healthcare workforce.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This proper training is especially important, given that we are also transforming the way we deliver healthcare services, from a hospital-centric to a people-centric model, and through an aggressive adoption of technology.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, can MOH provide an update on our preparations to ensure that our healthcare workforce have both the necessary hard skills and soft skills to care for the aged?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I would like to note my appreciation for our healthcare workers – nurses, doctors and medical social workers – for their hard work and dedication.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: However, is MOH also tracking the supply and number of doctors needed to meet the vast cross-section of healthcare demands in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: For example, are the sizes of the cohorts in the medical faculties in our universities calibrated such that the rate of supply of doctors in the profession would meet the needs of our population over the next 10, 20, 30 years?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Additionally, can MOH, in collaboration with the integrated healthcare clusters, provide guidance and regulations to prevent a disproportionately high number of qualified doctors from specialising in niche specialties?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This is because disproportionate over-specialisation may leave other specialties less well-staffed which will, in turn, lead to multiple healthcare needs not being met.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: The Breast Cancer Foundation conducted a nationwide survey last year and found that more than half of the 1,005 women aged 15 and above who were surveyed had limited knowledge of breast cancer.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Only 45% of the women did self-examination as well as went for medical check-ups.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: Early detection of breast cancer in the early stages of the disease offers a higher chance of survival.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: This is because breast cancer is one of the easiest cancers to beat, if found early.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: In order to further improve the early diagnosis of breast cancer, could MOH please enhance our national screening programme?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo
text: And how can MOH raise public awareness of breast cancer further?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Chairman, I am heartened to note that the number of unwanted pregnancies is decreasing in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Medical advances, the easing of stigma over unwed mothers, the availability of contraception, and the support available for unwed parents could be contributing factors for the decline in the numbers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Under the 1974 Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Bill, abortions are currently allowed up to 24 weeks of pregnancy without restriction.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This was based on the scientific norms of the time where 24 weeks were considered the justification age by which babies have a chance of survival.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The same Act of 1974 removed the previous stipulations of parental consent rallied round abortion and approval by the Termination of Pregnancy (ToP) Authorisation Board.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we look at the basis of the 1974 Termination of Pregnancy Act, we have progressed on many fronts since then.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have access to proper and high-quality healthcare.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Science and medical care have advanced greatly, too, and evidence shows that survival rates for extremely early pre-term babies have improved dramatically in the last 15 years.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A 2015 report in a New England Journal of Medicine also found that infants born at 22 weeks could have a good chance of survival without severe health problems if hospitals treated them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Termination of pregnancy is not an easy decision.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I remember still the words of a 68-year-old lady who told me, "The procedure itself did not hurt much but my heart has been aching for the last 47 years."

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: So, may I ask what is the Ministry doing to control gestational diabetes among women in Singapore?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Chairman, with your permission, may I display some slides?

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Singapore needs to prepare for a rapidly ageing population in the next one to two decades.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our vision is a Nation for All Ages, where all our citizens can age healthily, purposefully and gracefully in place.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Hence, we are investing efforts at three levels.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, at the individual level, we will create new options for ageing in place and empowering self-care.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Second, at the community level, we will build a strong community care system for seniors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And third, at the national level, we will develop enablers to better deliver care services for seniors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our models of care will need to evolve, as there is no one-size-fits-all option for seniors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH is working closely with MND, HDB and the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) to pilot new forms of housing developments that are twinned with care services and integrated within public housing estates.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will be our Singapore model for assisted living.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Both Ministries are already studying potential sites for such "assisted living" developments within public housing as well as in the private residential market.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Basic domestic services, such as housekeeping and 24/7 monitoring and response, could be offered to support independent living.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Home care could be layered on, as needed, for frail seniors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We are collaborating with the Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) and various agencies to explore how design interventions can help make our neighbourhoods age-friendly, as suggested by Ms Tin Pei Ling.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Standards, Productivity and Innovation Board (SPRING) Singapore also works with public agencies and private organisations to develop national standards to support active ageing and senior-friendly infrastructure design.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Beyond new "housing plus" models that combine housing with care, we also need to enhance current services to support the majority of seniors who are already staying in existing residential estates to age in place.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For seniors in ageing rental precincts who are unable to afford domestic help, for example, we had piloted the Care Close to Home (C2H) programme in 2014 where care services are provided out of SACs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Today, our Active Ageing Hubs (AAHs) provide a suite of care services for seniors as their needs evolve over time.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have started two AAHs at McNair and Kampung Admiralty, and will be opening three more in the Toa Payoh, Queenstown and Bukit Merah planning areas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Overall, I am encouraged to know that home and community care services have gained traction among seniors in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Around 14,000 clients have benefited from subsidised home and community care services as of late 2017, more than the 10,000 clients who had taken up subsidised nursing home places.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In fact, this has been the trend for the last three years.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will do more to support ageing in place in the coming months.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Today, seniors with complex medical conditions may be taking multiple medications prescribed by various doctors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: There is also the risk of non-compliance or medication errors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will launch a new community-based Pharmaceutical Care Services pilot so that, in the future, seniors can get help with their medications at community touchpoints, such as senior care centres, where community pharmacists will be stationed, saving them multiple trips to the doctor or hospital.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will start with a pool of some 20 pharmacists from our polyclinics and retail pharmacies, such as Guardian, Unity Pharmacy and Watsons.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This year, we will enhance the Seniors’ Mobility and Enabling Fund (SMF) to enable seniors with frailty to age confidently.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To date, we have disbursed close to $100 million since the launch of the scheme in 2011, with over 49,000 beneficiaries.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To lend more support to end-of-life care, we are extending SMF subsidies to clients on home palliative care services in the coming months.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will also review the SMF means-testing tiers for devices so that our subsidies remain effective and targeted at those who need help.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling asked for an update on Our National Innovation Challenge on Active and Confident Ageing.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I am pleased to report that we have launched six grant calls to date, with around $33 million awarded across 23 projects.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These include projects in areas, such as home monitoring solutions and assistive devices.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To improve care navigation, we are leveraging technology, which Miss Cheryl Chan spoke about, to develop a Health Marketplace.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Many consumers are already using e-platforms, such as "Amazon" and "Redmart".

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We hope to create an equivalent platform to make it easy for seniors and their caregivers to find, customise and order community-based eldercare services, such as home care, medical escorts and transport and meals on wheels.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They can do so via a mobile app and will also have the opportunity to give ratings on services and providers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We plan to collaborate with the industry to start a Health Marketplace over the next year or so.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We believe that it is also important to integrate seniors within supportive communities so that they do not feel isolated, as mentioned by Dr Lily Neo.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our goal is to build an inclusive “Kampong for All Ages” through the Community Networks for Seniors (CNS) programme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The Silver Generation Office (SGO) placed within AIC, also puts us in good stead through our SG Ambassadors to proactively reach out to new cohorts of Singaporeans aged 65 and above, bringing health and healthcare to them.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And where help is needed, various Government agencies and partners will come together to deliver coordinated care to the senior, closing the “social last mile” for our seniors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Ms K Thanaletchimi and Dr Lily Neo asked about the benefits of our integration efforts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The transfer of functions from MSF to MOH, including services under the SCNs, will be accompanied by a transfer of staff and resources.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This will allow MOH to plan and develop health and social support services for seniors more holistically.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The staging of SCN services already takes into account the demographics of each planning zone and will continue to do so.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The consolidation allows us to make the delivery of services more citizen-centric, increases productivity by minimising duplication and ensures that no needy senior falls between the cracks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will take the opportunity to review and inject more programming to enhance the SACs, such as conducting preventive health and wellness programmes, to keep seniors active and well in the community.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Ms Thanaletchimi also asked about a one-stop centre for all relevant senior services.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: AIC currently provides a one-stop service to help seniors and their caregivers navigate services and schemes in the community, with several touchpoints to facilitate this.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Many of our VWOs are also go-to points for seniors and caregivers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In parallel with our nationwide rollout of CNS, MOH will also invest in community nursing.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our healthcare clusters are doing more to support this shift to community care.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In the area of preventive health, for instance, community nurses can reach out to residents in the community and coach them to manage their health better.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: For residents who have been discharged from hospital and may have complex medical issues, the community nurse can provide direct care in their homes, for example, in wound care management.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: And for those in need of end-of-life care, they can be supported by community nurses trained in palliative care.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Senior Staff Nurse Noormala Hamid from the National Healthcare Group is one example.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Noormala is experienced in managing palliative care patients, and works closely with other healthcare professionals to coordinate care plans, administer medication and monitor patients at home.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: She serves as a bridge between her patients and their doctors, and also provides support to families and caregivers who experience the psychological and emotional challenges that come with end-of-life care.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: A strong community care system also includes community mental health.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked how we are making mental health services more accessible, while Assoc Prof Daniel Goh suggested a national dementia plan.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Dementia support has been a central component of our community mental health plan which I announced last year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have strengthened measures to provide care for persons with mental health conditions and dementia, including making services more accessible for them.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: AIC is the key agency that coordinates care and support of persons with mental health needs in the community across health and social care sectors, including SSOs.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: More than 1,900 individuals have benefited to date.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In addition, AIC has worked with social service partners to establish a network of 33 community outreach teams to reach out to persons at risk of depression or dementia.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: They also educate the public on mental health and dementia conditions as part of our outreach efforts.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: More than 140 GP partners have been trained to diagnose and support persons with mental health conditions in the community, supported by allied health-led community intervention teams.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To date, 16 of such teams have been established to support the GPs, community and grassroots organisations in caring for persons with mental health conditions.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To date, some 8,800 patients have also benefited from the Institute of Mental Health’s (IMH’s) post-discharge "after-care" support, transiting smoothly from hospital to home.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will continue to work closely with IMH to enhance its capability to monitor these patients post-discharge.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Similar to the Singapore Civil Defence Force Community First Responder app, AIC is developing a Dementia Friends mobile app to support seniors with dementia and their caregivers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We had initially considered building a national database of persons with dementia which Assoc Prof Daniel Goh spoke about.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: However, families we consulted preferred a voluntary approach where caregivers can register their loved ones.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Going forward, caregivers can do so by using the AIC's mobile app and also access useful resources.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Members of the public can also register as Dementia Friends to learn about the signs and symptoms of dementia and to help keep a look-out for persons with dementia who are lost or wandering.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We plan to launch this app later this year.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about how we will work with MSF to implement a change for Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) who need to apply for the FDW schemes.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will accept the Client Assessment Form which is already administered by disability care services, such as day activity centres, so that the PWDs need not have to go through an additional assessment.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Next, let me touch on our healthcare workforce, a critical enabler in achieving our vision for community care.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Given the twin challenges of rising demand for healthcare and slowing local labour force growth, we need to ensure the sustainability of the healthcare workforce over the long term.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our approach, as reflected in our Healthcare Manpower Plan 2020, must be to equip our healthcare workforce with future skills to provide better care, achieve higher productivity in healthcare and grow a strong local core.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The growing healthcare industry offers good jobs, and we are stepping up efforts to attract more locals into the sector, from school leavers to mid-career professionals as well as older workers.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: To attract more mid-career Singaporeans into the nursing profession, I announced last month that NUS Nursing will launch a two-year Bachelor of Science (Nursing) Programme later this year under the PCP for Registered Nurses (PCP-RN) and will complement the existing PCP-RN at Nanyang Polytechnic.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I agree with Ms Joan Pereira and Ms Thanaletchimi that the silver workforce is an important resource and can be an engine for national development.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Today, more than nine in 10 public sector healthcare professionals who reach the age of 62 are re-employed, and we will do more to attract seniors without prior healthcare experience into the sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This includes over 40 professionals who made a career switch to the community care sector in 2017 under the Senior Management Associate Scheme.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Henry Kwek and Ms Thanaletchimi asked about our plans to develop the healthcare workforce as we grow the sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling also asked for an update on the training and career pathways for nurses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH has been working closely with SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) to develop a Skills Framework for nurses, allied health professionals as well as support care staff to facilitate a national recognition of skills in the healthcare industry and development of career progression pathways as well as remuneration frameworks.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is targeted to be developed by the end of this year, and we will be engaging employers and the healthcare union on its adoption.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I note that Ms Thanaletchimi has also called for the formation of an Association for the ILTC sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As Senior Minister of State Lam Pin Min mentioned in Parliament on 1 March, we already have existing structures in place to promote collaboration among sectoral bodies, AIC and MOH, and will continue to strengthen existing partnerships as well as build new ones.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH will be investing in developing a more robust Continuing Education and Training (CET) system, which is skills-based and industry-focused, for our nursing profession to complement pre-employment training in a few ways.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: First, we want to develop a more comprehensive and coordinated system of upgrading to higher qualifications.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We will collaborate with our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) and healthcare institutions to design skills-based, modularised and stackable courses for our nurses that can add up, over time, to higher qualifications.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Both the Nanyang Polytechnic and Ngee Ann Polytechnic have introduced part-time skills deepening programmes, such as the Specialist Diplomas in nursing gerontology, community gerontology and clinical education.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As of end 2017, about 90 nurses have enrolled in the three specialist diploma courses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Later this year, NUS Nursing will introduce a new part-time and modular graduate diploma in Community Health Nursing to equip nurses with the clinical skills to manage population health needs in the community, including clinical decision-making and chronic disease management.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Second, we want to build a more robust system of in-employment training across the acute as well as ILTC sectors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Given the dynamic healthcare landscape, our nurses will have to continue to learn and deepen their skills on the job.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This may mean that a stronger national skills credentialing capability will have to be built.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Third, we want to nurture and build up stronger institutions for nursing education.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As a start, we will be working with NUS Nursing to strengthen the nexus of its curriculum with practice, by forming a new advisory council comprising key nursing leaders from both the acute and community care sectors.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: In the future, we envisage new national centres of excellence in specific areas of specialised nursing education that will train practising nurses across the various healthcare clusters in specific skills, such as geriatric care.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Taken together, we hope to build a first-class nursing education system that can empower our nurses with deep skills and give them the confidence to be at the forefront of driving care transformation.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: During last week's Budget Debate, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong called for an increase in the salaries of our local nurses, citing a lag when benchmarked against the pay ratios in other countries.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The median monthly income for full-time employed residents had included employer's Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions, but the amount cited for registered nurses had not.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: If we exclude employer's CPF contributions for both, the local ratio is, in fact, not 1.06 but 1.2, which is actually comparable to the pay ratio in Australia, as quoted by Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: However, as workforce demographics and income profiles vary across countries, benchmarking purely based on pay ratios is not meaningful.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Over the years, we have reviewed the salaries of nurses, which have increased in tandem with their expanding roles and responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Beyond pay, we have also enhanced professional development and career advancement opportunities for our nurses.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Through these efforts, we are encouraged that our nursing intakes have increased by 30% over the past five years and the proportion of males in nursing has also risen from 8% to 10% during the same period.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: I am personally inspired by the experience of Dr Pauline Tan.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Currently CEO of Yishun Community Hospital, Pauline started out as an enrolled nurse at the age of 18, and actively pursued training opportunities to upgrade her skills and knowledge.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Over the years, she has made invaluable contributions in various roles within the healthcare sector.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Pauline is testament to the capabilities and potential of our nurses and the many career progression pathways available.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: As we deepen the skills and capabilities of our nurses and other healthcare professionals, we can also enhance their scope of practice to support the implementation of more person-centred care models.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Today, all prescriptions drafted by nurses and pharmacists require a doctor's counter-signature.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Diagnosed with prostate cancer in July last year, he was referred to a home palliative care team upon discharge.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: With the introduction of collaborative prescribing rights, Mr Tan’s palliative care nurse can assess his condition and issue the prescription for antibiotics, for example, saving his caregiver an additional trip just to collect the prescription.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We recognise the need to also upskill our allied health workforce, as highlighted by Mr Christopher de Souza.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: MOH and our public healthcare institutions have established various initiatives and grants to support the training and development of our allied health professionals (AHPs).

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: These include skills attachments, postgraduate qualifications, and fellowships in clinical, education and management-related areas.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: We have been supporting the development of close to 250 AHPs annually.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Our therapy support staff are an equally important group who work alongside therapists to provide rehabilitation care to patients.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: The new apprenticeship-based diploma, where a majority of the training is conducted in partnership with the employers, allows newly hired and in-service therapy assistants to take on larger roles to provide rehabilitation care to seniors, and progression in their careers as senior therapy assistants.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: Mr Alex Yam asked whether MOH will be reviewing the abortion time limit.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This upper gestational limit of 24 weeks for abortions is based on scientific evidence of foetal viability outside the womb.

speaker: Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan
text: This is also supported by international studies and professional bodies.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, when the Prime Minister spoke about the War on Diabetes during his National Day Rally last year, there were some questions why this topic warranted such a high level of attention.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It does not matter how much money one makes or receives in the SG Bonus.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Without good health, it is useless having lots of money.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: That is why, during Chinese New Year, I always wish my residents and friends good health, "身体健康" and people always respond that that is the best and most important blessing they desire.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: However, I am glad to note that people do not just wish for good health blessings.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Many have taken heed of the call to fight and prevent diabetes.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: There are now healthier food options available at buffet spreads and I have seen many taking the effort to exercise more regularly, with quite a few looking reasonably slimmer, fitter and better.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It is a lifelong condition and takes a dedicated effort to keep it under control.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The beautiful part of it is that regular exercise and controlled diet can also help fight other chronic conditions like high blood pressure and high cholesterol levels.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: What are the challenges faced and what is the plan to sustain awareness and translation into action over the long term?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Our children and young people are increasingly overweight.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister give us a report of progress from the front?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: What are our new and continuing efforts, plans, strategies and tactics?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: In this connection, could the Ministry explore avenues for working with the food manufacturing industry and the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) to apply existing incentives and support local food manufacturers to release low-sugar snacks and drinks?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The Industry Transformation Map (ITM) for food manufacturing is more advanced than most other ITMs and seems well-placed to develop and promote low-sugar products on an industry basis.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Our family doctors, I am sure everyone will agree, are at the frontlines of healthcare in our community.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Often, they are the first point of contact for medical intervention by patients and their families, and patients and their families have also built a relationship with them.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Family doctors are thus usually in the best position to provide patient-centric care as they have a comprehensive overview of their patients' physical and mental health conditions and, to varying degrees, the context as well.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: They play an important role in complex care needs, such as case management and preventive care.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: These will help lower our escalating healthcare expenditure due to our ageing population.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Can MOH provide an update on the progress of and future plans for primary care transformation in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In view of the fast-changing medical and IT development, the intention on repealing it is timely, to align MOH's priority and better safeguard patients' interests.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Embracing IT is necessary for the provision of medical care at a higher level of proficiency and efficiency.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Having this new Bill will also improve governance of healthcare providers and ensure continuity of care and accountability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope MOH will be thorough and will not leave out any inadequacy of governance to tackle unfavourable healthcare practices that have no recourse with the present Act.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This will ensure that the new Bill will be relevant and encompassing.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I favour the NEHR system because health records follow the patients.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This means convenience for patients and accuracy of medical information, without them having to repeat their medical histories and medications at every visit to a clinic.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is especially important in emergency settings when patients cannot relate.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I want to share the challenges I face when I adopted a clinic IT system that contributes to NEHR in my clinic last year.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: My very first concern was what happens if the IT system should suddenly fail, a possibility from any computer or IT glitches?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I stand to lose all the medical records of my patients.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: It was just as well that I continued manually writing and recording on the usual hard copies whilst I entered electronically entailing double work.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There is also another concern of late, that of cyber security.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: NEHR also needs getting accustomed to, even if the staff and nurses are IT-savvy, thus they have to be retrained, entailing expenses on the adoption of NEHR.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: When MOH rolls out NEHR more widely, I hope the above challenges can be addressed to ease its adoption.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There will be patients who prefer to opt-out from NEHR record sharing for various personal reasons.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope MOH will give flexibility of choice that includes opt-out options to those who request.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: The Government will also need to step up its surveillance in this regard.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: Smugglers are increasingly creative due to the attractive profits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Lam Pin Min)
text: Mr Chairman, may I have your permission to display some slides during my speech?

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Minister Gan has highlighted efforts to ensure healthcare remains accessible, affordable and is of good quality.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I will now elaborate on how we are developing capabilities and capacity for the future, ensuring that Singaporeans have access to good care close to their homes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The cornerstone of a sustainable healthcare system is strong primary care, where patients with chronic conditions are managed well in the community, with better health outcomes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Residents in the West and Central regions can also look forward to new polyclinics.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Redeveloped Bedok and Ang Mo Kio polyclinics opened in July 2017 and January 2018 respectively.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The redeveloped Yishun Polyclinic will open in mid-2018.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu has asked for updates on our primary care transformation efforts.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are investing more resources to support our GP partners, through the PCN scheme.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: PCNs are networks of GPs delivering care via multidisciplinary teams comprising doctors, nurses and primary care coordinators, who provide holistic care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We hope to eventually see 50% of CHAS GP clinics on board the scheme.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I have shared MOH’s vision for primary care, which is "One Singaporean, One Family Doctor" in previous COS debates.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The PCN scheme complements our efforts to encourage trusting, long-term relationships between doctors and their patients.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This continuous follow-up has allowed Dr Kwong to gain a deeper understanding of her needs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For example, Mdm Siti’s high blood pressure was detected early as Dr Kwong had advised her to screen for other chronic conditions, as part of the plan in managing her diabetes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: She received advice on her diet and lifestyle activities from the PCN nurse, as well as utilised diabetic eye and foot screening services provided by the PCN team.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The PCN care coordinator also ensured her appointments were well-coordinated.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I am heartened by the strong rapport and trust forged among Mdm Siti, Dr Kwong and the PCN care team, and encourage all Singaporeans to have a regular family doctor today.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To augment our Primary Care sector, we are also increasing capacity across various settings to ensure appropriate and seamless care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Since 2010, we have opened or expanded five hospital facilities, namely, Ng Teng Fong General Hospital, CGH-St Andrew's Community Hospital Integrated Building, Jurong Community Hospital, Yishun Community Hospital and Khoo Teck Puat General Hospital.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The development of three more hospitals are underway.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Sengkang General and Community Hospitals will open by the second half of 2018, while Outram Community Hospital will open progressively by 2020.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Hospital bed capacity will increase further when the Integrated Care Hub at Novena and the Woodlands General and Community Hospitals open by 2022.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In addition, the National Centre for Infectious Diseases will progressively open from end-2018.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Aged care capacity will be increased to meet the demands of an ageing population.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There are also plans to increase the number of nursing home beds from the current 14,900 to 17,000.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In tandem with the increase in infrastructure capacity is the need to ensure sufficient manpower.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked if we are calibrating the training pipeline for specialists to meet medium- to long-term needs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have increased the proportion of residency positions offered to specialties that are in greater need to address the demands of an ageing population.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The number of residency positions taken up in Advanced Internal Medicine, Rehabilitation Medicine and Geriatric Medicine have doubled from 4% of the total residency intake in 2013 to 8% in 2017.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH does regular reviews to calibrate the number of residency positions for each specialty, based on our projected needs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH also periodically reviews the training requirements to ensure relevance to our local context.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This includes instituting a mandatory Geriatric Medicine Modular Training Programme to equip residents with the skills to manage elderly patients.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, we cannot indefinitely increase capacity and manpower.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have thus embarked on efforts to improve our care delivery.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Chen Show Mao and Mr Baey Yam Keng have asked for updates on the War on Diabetes (WoD).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is a whole-of-nation effort where everyone has a role to play.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH is developing a Patient Empowerment for Self-care Framework to empower people with diabetes to initiate and sustain lifestyle changes with the support of healthcare professionals, community-based providers and other forms of social support.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Under this framework, there will be a National Curriculum developed with educational materials for patients, caregivers and the public, and resources which healthcare professionals and community-based providers can use for patient empowerment.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The first tranche of the materials will be available by mid-2018.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH is currently enhancing our diabetes management programmes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As part of the Disease Management Workgroup, set up under the National Diabetes Prevention and Care Taskforce, we have rolled out initiatives targeted at eye and kidney complications.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will now address diabetic foot complications, as diabetes is the most common cause of non-traumatic lower extremity amputations (LEAs).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: (In Mandarin):   If diabetes is not treated early or managed well, there may be long-term complications, such as blindness, kidney failure and LEA.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In 2015, for every 100,000 adult Singaporeans with diabetes, about 180 had an LEA, which is much higher than the OECD average.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH will be setting up a workgroup to develop a strategy to reduce diabetes-related amputations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The workgroup will review the national landscape of the diabetic foot services provided to patients with diabetes, make recommendations for the national care guidelines, and review the roles and training needs of healthcare professionals involved in diabetic foot care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Through improving the quality of care services, we can promptly detect foot problems among patients with diabetes and start treatment immediately to avoid amputations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: (In English): Chairman, WoD is a shared responsibility.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have thus provided funding to support cluster-led, community-based diabetes prevention and management programmes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In the East, CGH has worked with the East Coast Group Representation Constituency (GRC) to train volunteers as Health Peers to motivate residents with, or at risk of, diabetes towards behavioural change.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Later this year, NUHS will launch the Patient Activation through Community Empowerment/Engagement for Diabetes Management (PACE-D) programme in the West where patients will be assigned to dedicated multidisciplinary care teams who will support them to take on proactive roles in disease management and lifestyle changes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Even as we develop new initiatives, we need to ensure the delivery of safe and quality care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Ms Sylvia Lim has asked about how hospital complaints on patient care are handled.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Hospitals have their own Hospital Quality Service/Patient Relations Office to deal with such complaints, and patients’ inputs are sought as part of the review process.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mediation is another avenue for patients and their families to resolve their disputes with hospitals.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Complaints escalated by patients to MOH are taken seriously and assessed in an independent manner for potential breach of the Private Hospitals and Medical Clinics Act.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: A formal investigation will be initiated by the Regulatory, Compliance and Enforcement Division against the hospital once a potential breach is identified.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The independent investigation by MOH will include opinion from the relevant appointed experts, and interviewing all parties related to the case, including the patients and their next-of-kin.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Under the Private Hospitals and Medical Clinics Act (PHMCA), institutions are required to report occurrences of Serious Reportable Events (SREs) to MOH and establish quality assurance committees (QACs) to review these SREs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Investigation reports are submitted to the Clinical Quality, Performance and Technology Division under the Healthcare Performance Group of MOH.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The priorities of this Division include Quality Assurance, Patient Safety systems and Quality improvement.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: One of the Division’s foci is to leverage the reported serious events for improvement and cross-institution learning opportunities, similar to the approach of the UK’s Healthcare Safety Investigation Branch.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Anonymised information is shared amongst the healthcare institutions, and forums are organised for healthcare institutions to discuss gap closure measures.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To future-proof our healthcare system, it is important that our laws stay current and flexible.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It will also appropriately regulate non-premise-based services, particularly as we want to encourage the outreach of community healthcare services, such as home medical services.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Regulatory clarity will be enhanced to make it easier for providers to understand and, therefore, comply with the legislative requirements.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: New requirements and competency mandates will also be introduced, including an additional governance layer called the Clinical Governance Officer, to provide technical oversight over more complex services, such as clinical laboratories and radiological services.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Fundamentally, the new Bill will allow MOH to strengthen its legislative powers to achieve our primary regulatory objective of safeguarding patient safety and welfare, as well as continuity of care.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Such powers include prescribing a list of prohibited unsafe practices that providers cannot offer, as well as mandatory participation of all healthcare service providers in the National Electronic Healthcare Records (NEHR).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have actively consulted stakeholders on the proposed policies in the new Bill and I am heartened by the generally positive feedback received.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Licensees appreciated the flexibility of the licensing approach to accommodate various care models.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The public was also supportive of the enhanced powers in the Bill to have "step-in" rights, tighter publicity controls and prohibition of unsafe practices.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Specifically, on the mandatory contribution of summary clinical data to NEHR, licensees and members of the public were generally supportive, and provided feedback on aspects, such as the cost of digitisation, opt-out procedures and patient confidentiality issues.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Dr Lily Neo has asked about patients who may prefer to opt out of NEHR.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are also studying a proposal when patient's future records will not be stored in NEHR at all.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, patients should note that this will cause a permanent gap in their medical record history.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To support licensees in this journey, MOH and the Integrated Health Information System (IHiS) have introduced financial, technical and clinical support to help licensees.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Even with the introduction of the new Bill, current regulations may not be flexible enough for the emergence of innovative care models.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: During the pilot, MOH will ensure that these businesses maintain essential safeguards for patient safety, while relaxing certain regulatory requirements or introducing new ones.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Thereafter, successful pilots will be mainstreamed under the Healthcare Services Bill with appropriate regulatory requirements.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: More details will be announced in the coming months.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang has asked about how precision medicine can be harnessed for patients' benefit.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Worldwide, we have seen how precision medicine treatments can be costly without strong evidence for improved health outcomes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Our end objective must be to support the development of precision medicine for positive health and economic outcomes.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To this end, MOH is coordinating a multi-agency effort to develop an integrated national strategy for precision medicine research and its subsequent implementation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This includes looking at enabling infrastructure, regulatory and ethical frameworks, as well as public education.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will provide a thorough update at an appropriate time.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: MOH also ensures that human biomedical research is carried out ethically.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Gene editing is presently used in basic research in Singapore and is governed by the Human Biomedical Research Act, and guidelines issued by the Bioethics Advisory Committee and National Medical Ethics Committee.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang has also asked about the standards for the provision of clinical genetic testing.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The sector will be given a sufficient ramp-up period before the standards become legally enforceable.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Part of developing a future-ready outlook is the task of preparing for anticipated healthcare challenges.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Overuse of antimicrobials, such as antibiotics, in the human, animal and agricultural sectors has exacerbated the problem of infection-causing microorganisms developing drug resistance.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is an international issue as drug-resistant microorganisms in other countries can easily spread across borders into Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), Singapore will continue to promote cooperation and innovative collaboration to strengthen ASEAN's resilience against AMR.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Besides AMR control, vaccination is important to prevent infection and reduce the risk of infectious disease outbreaks.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Leon Perera has asked about MOH’s approach towards subsidising vaccinations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To ensure collective population-level protection or herd immunity and encourage vaccine uptake, childhood vaccinations against highly infectious diseases with community outbreak potential, such as measles, are fully subsidised at the polyclinics.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For diseases with low community outbreak potential, for example, Human Papillomavirus (HPV)-related diseases, vaccination is recommended for personal protection.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The National Adult Immunisation Schedule was introduced on 1 November 2017 to provide guidance on the recommended vaccinations that persons 18 years and older should receive, and MediSave use is allowed for these recommended vaccinations.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I urge all Singaporeans and healthcare providers to partner us in these initiatives to make our healthcare system better and keep Singaporeans healthier.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Chairman, the Government hospitals and clinics are one of the best sources for reliable and impartial information on healthcare.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: This can empower our elderly and their caregivers with very helpful information and help them better manage their health and their lifestyle, so that they can live a good quality life for as long as possible.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: It is also very encouraging to see how drinks manufacturers have responded in support of such a move.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Also, habits are cultivated from young and it is important that our children start their lives with the right habits.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We are encouraging greater personal responsibility for healthy living, and community partnerships to make healthy living more accessible and sustainable for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: I will touch on three key areas – the War on Diabetes (WoD), health promotion efforts for all, particularly seniors and ethnic minorities, and tobacco control.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Mr Chen Show Mao and Mr Baey Yam Keng asked for updates on WoD.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan spoke about helping Singaporeans lead a healthy lifestyle.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We will continue to support all Singaporeans, regardless of economic and socioeconomic backgrounds, to eat healthily, be screened and exercise as part of our WoD.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: HPB’s Healthier Dining Programme offers more affordable, delicious and nutritious food options.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: In addition to food courts and restaurants, we have extended the Healthier Dining Programme to coffee shops and hawker centres in December 2016.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We now have healthier mee soto, chapatti and carrot cake, just to name a few.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: So, yes, you can have your cake – just make sure that it is a healthier cake – and eat it, too.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Mr Chen Show Mao asked for an update on plans to develop low-sugar food and drinks locally.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: In July 2017, HPB launched the Healthier Ingredients Development Scheme (HIDS) to build our food sector’s capabilities to innovate and produce new healthier food products, like healthier oils, rice and noodles.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: With support from HIDS, Mr Desmond Goh from People Bee Hoon invested in R&D, marketing and trade promotion of new wholegrain healthier bee hoon.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Sales of Chili Brand wholegrain bee hoon doubled over the past months.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This means that more families are buying, cooking and eating healthier bee hoon.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We will be further extending the HIDS grant to include sugar-sweetened beverages, desserts and sauces.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We are working with MTI, through the Economic Development Board (EDB) and SPRING Singapore, to align our industry efforts, including through the ITM for food processing.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Together, we will spur businesses to innovate and market new healthier food products.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling asked about the efforts to promote lower consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) and to help young children develop healthier dietary habits.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Current efforts, such as the Healthier Choice Symbol (HCS) and the Healthy Meals in Preschools Programme, have shown encouraging results.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Under the NurtureSG initiative, we have partnered the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) to ensure all preschools only serve drinks with the HCS symbols from 1 January 2018.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We are studying sugar-reduction measures from other countries, such as the UK and France.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The UK and France have implemented colour-coded front-of-pack labels for food and drinks.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The UK uses traffic light colours to tell consumers whether a food item has high, medium or low amounts of nutrients, such as sugar and saturated fats.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: France has Nutri-score which scores the nutrient content of food and drinks.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Some countries have implemented a tax on SSBs to encourage manufacturers to reformulate their drinks and reduce the sugar content.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: In March 2016, the UK announced a 2-tiered levy on pre-packaged beverages.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The purpose is not to raise revenue but to encourage product reformulation.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Although the levy only takes effect in April 2018, the UK authorities have shared with us that more than 40% of affected products have been reformulated.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: MOH will carefully review this and other measures to encourage product reformulation and conduct a public consultation before deciding our next steps.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Moving on to screening, if discovered early, interventions, such as diet and exercise, can prevent pre-diabetes from worsening.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Younger Singaporeans are advised to go for diabetes screening if they are at higher risk of having diabetes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Risk factors include a family history of Type 2 diabetes, overweight or high blood pressure.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We are helping Singaporeans between 18 and 39 to assess their risk for diabetes through the Diabetes Risk Assessment (DRA) on HPB's HealthHub app.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: To date, the DRA tool has been used about 116,000 times by younger Singaporeans.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Those identified as high-risk for diabetes should go for medical screening.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: For those above 40, they should go for regular diabetes screening once every three years and they can benefit from subsidies under the Screen for Life initiative.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Moving on to stepping up to the challenge of an active lifestyle.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: On active lifestyle, we have made strides in the first two seasons of the National Steps Challenge.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: HPB has rolled out the third season in October last year.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: More than 650,000 people have signed up and clocked more than 260 billion steps.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This is equivalent to 200 million kilometres (km) or more than 5,000 times around the Equator!

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We are working with SportSG to organise more fun social physical activities for all ages so that Singaporeans can have access to them at various community and workplace settings.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: On the second area of health promotion efforts for seniors and minorities, on seniors, I agree with Miss Cheryl Chan that we need sustainable preventive health efforts to address the needs of an ageing population and we have stepped up efforts to improve healthy living in this aspect.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Through the Community Network for Seniors (CNS), HPB, with support from Silver Generation Ambassadors, has implemented several active ageing programmes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Community Health Posts, located in the neighbourhoods, offer health screenings, regular health coaching and lifestyle follow-up for seniors to help manage chronic conditions better.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Thirdly, we have started senior-centric exercise programmes, such as Zumba Gold and FIT+, and mass workout sessions under the Community Physical Activity Programmes (CPAP).

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Ms Joan Pereira suggested that the Ministry review information on diabetes management and diet for elderly patients and their caregivers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The Patient Empowerment for Self-Care Framework aims to help Singaporeans with diabetes initiate and sustain lifestyle changes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: On health promotion among ethnic minorities, we are seeing greater awareness among Malay and Indian communities on health matters but there is more to do.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The key thing is that "healthier choice" is decided based on whether that category of food is lower in terms of sugar or other not too healthy things.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Is it healthier for that food band or for that food category?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: (In Malay):   Last August, I visited popular comedian Alias Kadir.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Alias had to undergo a surgery to amputate his lower leg due to diabetes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: He already had diabetes when he was in his 40s, but he did not seek treatment.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: After the surgery, however, Alias was determined to change.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: He also wanted all of us to learn from his experience – that we must always take care before something goes wrong with us.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: And if something does go wrong, we must not underestimate the importance of taking medications and watching what we eat, as well as remembering to go for follow-ups with doctors to manage diabetes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We are working with many community partners to help the Malay community stay healthy at each stage of life.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We have taken steps to collaborate with caterers to slowly change the way we eat at the community level.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: For instance, we are working with the Singapore Halal Culinary Federation (SHCF) and caterers, such as Eternally Yours and Jamil Catering, so that they can provide healthier halal food choices.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Through this effort, it is hoped that the community can gradually grow to like healthy food that can still taste delicious.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Step Two – Towards Mosques as Health Movers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Taking care of our health is part of our religious obligations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We hope that this initiative will grow and reach 20 mosques by the end of this year.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Hence, what will be done at these mosques?

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The mosques will provide services to help diabetes sufferers manage their condition, undergo health screening, and conduct physical activities.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We are heartened to see more mosques joining this initiative.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: For instance, Al-Mawaddah Mosque sent their canteen staff to attend culinary training organised by HPB so that healthier dishes can be served at the mosque.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Our hope is that healthy yet delicious food is served at all mosques, be it for gatherings, breaking of fast, Hari Raya celebrations and so on.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The mosques should be the health movers of the Muslim community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Step Three – Towards a Community That Loves Exercising.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We will add more spaces and opportunities for our Malay community to exercise or engage in physical activities.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: For example, I launched the "Get Fit for Umrah" initiative, which encourages pilgrims to build up their fitness before performing their umrah (minor pilgrimage).

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This is done with the support of TM Fouzy Travel and Tours last year.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We will scale up this programme so that more umrah and haj pilgrims can benefit from it.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: HPB will be working with the Association of Muslim Travel Agents Singapore (AMTAS) to include more Muslim travel agencies that can also offer this initiative.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: In addition to having a good reputation as disciplined pilgrims in Mecca and Medina, our Singapore pilgrims will also be known as healthy and fit pilgrims!

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: They participated in the four health conversation sessions "Awak Ok?" ("Are You OK?") at Geylang, Jurong, Tampines and Woodlands; they worked out together, for example, at the Zumba sessions at Tampines Hub; and they also rolled up their sleeves – like the doctors, nurses and partners from Muslim Healthcare Professional Association (MHPA).

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: So, let us work together to build a community that is active, fit and healthy!

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: (In English): Community organisations like the Hindu Endowments Board and the Singapore Indian Development Association (SINDA) are actively promoting healthy living to the Indian community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We want to complement and build on these efforts in three ways.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Third, we will leverage social networks to train Health Ambassadors and equip them with skills to actively reach out to and promote healthier living to their families and friends.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The final key focus area of my speech is tobacco control.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We will re-emphasise the harms of environmental tobacco smoke and the harms of tobacco.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We will have a ground-up campaign involving youths in schools and IHLs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: HPB will also work with partners, such as the Singapore Cancer Society and the Football Association of Singapore and other partners, to reach out to all and, in particular, youths on social media, in schools and other places.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We will continue to enhance our smoking cessation services to support smokers on their tobacco-free journey.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: HPB will engage more workplaces, such as taxi and bus transportation sectors, to help their employees to quit smoking.
